For less common cases where this independence does not hold, we instead estimate a configuration-independent twist subspace of higher dimension that contains the local feasible subspaces, allowing the same fixed-gain strategy to be used. Experiments across simulated and real-world single- and multi-DoF objects show that the proposed method consistently reduces constraint-violating contact loads relative to isotropic impedance control while maintaining task execution.

title: Driving, Fast or Slow? Neuro-Symbolic Guidance for Motion Prediction in Multi-Modal Ground Mobility
abstract: Accurate and interpretable motion prediction for heterogeneous traffic spaces, including pedestrians, bicycles, cars, and buses, is essential for safe autonomous navigation. Nevertheless, state-of-the-art approaches remain predominantly black-box, lacking explicit encoding of the regulatory and behavioral constraints of real-world mobility. We propose Trajectory Compliance-Shaping (TraCS), a neuro-symbolic framework that augments existing black-box forecasting backbones with interpretable and probabilistic first-order logic. To do so, TraCS employs an agentic code-generation pipeline to bridge the gap between natural-language descriptions of traffic regulations and probabilistic motion prediction. Furthermore, TraCS employs a reactive data-streaming inference engine that maintains and efficiently updates compliance landscapes as scenes evolve. To prevent TraCS from overconfidently steering the backbone's predictions in the wrong direction, we propose a neural confidence rating learned as a context-aware attenuation of the compliance signal. We demonstrate on the Argoverse 2 benchmark how TraCS consistently improves state-of-the-art prediction backbones, showing that probabilistic and symbolic compliance reasoning is a broadly applicable complement for aligning purely neural motion predictors in safety-critical applications.

title: T(R,O) Grasp++: Cross-Embodiment Dexterous Grasping in Cluttered Environments at Scale
abstract: Dexterous grasping in cluttered scenes remains a central challenge in robotic manipulation, as it requires high-dimensional hand coordination under complex object-environment constraints. To address this problem, we introduce one of the largest simulation benchmarks to date, comprising around 0.5B grasp annotations across eight dexterous hands and approximately 50K objects. Furthermore, we propose T(R,O) Grasp++, a scalable diffusion-based framework for cross-embodiment dexterous grasp synthesis in cluttered environments. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms existing baselines, achieving an average success rate of 88% across eight dexterous embodiments. Meanwhile, our pipeline achieves only 0.3s inference latency while improving inference sample efficiency by over 10 times.

title: Eye, Robot: Learning Expressive Gaze Dynamics via a VLM-Guided Transformer-VAE
abstract: Gaze plays a crucial role in human communication, conveying intent, emotion, and vitality through subtle eye and head movements. However, realistic gaze behaviors in humanoid robots are often constrained by task-specific controllers, such as object tracking systems, resulting in rigid, unnatural motion that lacks human-like expressiveness. In this work, we propose a VLM-guided framework for a facial robot that decouples high-level cognitive reasoning from low-level motor control, with a action head learned directly from human motion data. A Vision-Language Model interprets the scene and designates gaze targets that condition our action head, the Realistic Gaze Transformer (RGT). Built on a Transformer-VAE, RGT is first pre-trained on human motion sequences in a self-supervised manner to learn a compact latent representation of full-head dynamics, then fine-tuned autoregressively for stable long-horizon rollouts under closed-loop deployment. At inference, conditioned on a brief motion history and the VLM-directed eyeball trajectory, RGT generates real-time 11-DoF commands synthesizing fluid eye–head coordination, eyelid motion, and natural blinking. By separating motion realism from gaze targeting, our framework preserves task-directed gaze while enhancing naturalness, yielding robot gaze that is both purposeful and imbued with the subtle vitality of human eye contact.

title: InfiniDanceRobot: A Streaming and Closed-Loop Music-driven Dance Generation for Humanoid Robot
abstract: Responding to rhythm is a natural human behaviour but a challenge of high-dynamic whole-body control for humanoid robots. Existing motion generation models produce expressive but physically invalid trajectories. As a result, even an expert-trained tracker accumulates a feasibility gap on long sequences of generated dance. In this work, we present InfiniDanceRobot, a latent-guided closed-loop system that streams music-conditioned dance directly to a physical humanoid robot. We collect about 50 hours of dance: 30 hours of lab-controlled motion capture data and 20 hours filtered from public datasets. To provide continuous motion generation ability, we propose a planner building on diffusion forcing with a causal receding noise schedule and cross-modal alignment. Then the latent-guided closed-loop optimization framework is designed to correct next-token predictions from tracker feedback during both training and inference. Experiments show that InfiniDanceRobot can generate expert human dance for the robot, producing continuous, physically plausible, and high-dynamic motion across diverse music styles and dance genres.

title: FACA: Force-Aware Contact Adaptation for Task-Parameterized Robotic Assembly
abstract:
Enabling robots to adapt across related contact-rich assembly tasks remains challenging. Policies trained in simulation with diverse geometries and task parameters often degrade under real execution due to contact-model mismatch, residual alignment error, friction variation, and force-response differences. We introduce FACA, a task-residual factorized contact world model for parameterized axial assembly. FACA separates known nominal task descriptors from hidden execution-time contact residuals. The task descriptor defines the nominal assembly prior, including clearance, part scale, insertion depth, and task type, while recent force/contact history, proprioception, and action history update a latent contact belief over residual contact state. This belief conditions task-dependent latent dynamics, value estimation, and action selection, and future rollout proceeds from the belief state without assuming access to future measured force.
We evaluate FACA on a compact but controlled axial assembly family rather than claiming full AutoMate benchmark coverage. The experiments are organized along two axes: generalization across known task parameters and adaptation to hidden residual/contact variations that are not provided as privileged inputs. When target-domain data are available, sparse autonomous rollouts or human correction snippets are used only as transition data to calibrate a lightweight residual dynamics adapter while keeping the base task-conditioned model and policy fixed. The experiments test whether FACA can better handle continuous task-parameter changes and difficult-to-encode contact residuals under the same low-level control interface.

title: TRIAD Planner : Three-Level Robust Imitation Learning for Autonomous Driving
abstract: Imitation learning for autonomous driving suffers from distribution shift between logged expert trajectories and self-induced deployment states. In Transformer-based planners, this shift can appear as excessive ego-state attention concentration, incomplete scene understanding, and unsafe mode selection under interaction uncertainty. This paper presents a robust imitation-learning planner based on a three-level robustness formulation. 1) Channel-level robustness: constrained ego-state attention to limit excessive concentration on a small subset of state channels. 2) Scene-level robustness: offline vision-language model (VLM) guidance to encourage the ego query to retain interaction-critical agent evidence and route-relevant map evidence. 3) Decision-level robustness: training-time multimodal supervision reshaped with a tail-risk score based on mean excess above Value at Risk. The scene-level VLM guidance and decision-level tail-risk supervision are used only during training, and the deployed planner incurs no additional inference-time overhead. On nuPlan test14, the proposed planner achieves the strongest performance among the evaluated learning-based methods and improves over CAR Planner, a strong constrained-attention imitation-learning baseline. On test14-hard, TRIAD Planner achieves NR-CLS and R-CLS of 73.39 and 67.12, compared with CAR Planner's reported 72.94 and 64.90, respectively. Ablation results show that combining all three-level components yields consistent performance across diverse scenarios, supporting the effectiveness of robust imitation learning for autonomous driving.

title: Collaborative Planning for UAV-UGV Teams under Operational Constraints via Masked Error-bounded Neuro-Symbolic Diffusion
abstract:
Collaborative planning under operational constraints is essential for heterogeneous robot teams in large-scale missions.
Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) provide rapid area coverage but are limited by onboard energy, while Unmanned Ground Vehicles (UGVs) can serve as mobile recharging stations yet are constrained by road-network traversability. Effective collaboration must enforce operational constraints during execution while enabling parallel, coordinated actions. Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) have shown promise through token unmasking but have two key limitations: entropy-guided scheduling assumes distributional alignment and reliance on differentiable constraints for diffusion-time optimization. We propose Masked Error-bounded Neuro-Symbolic Diffusion (MEND), which formulates collaborative planning as a conditional masked generative process to generate context-aware action sequences for UAV-UGV teams. MEND introduces a neuro-symbolic diffusion paradigm that constrains conditional masked diffusion policies at execution by reweighting the learned action distribution with a logic-induced admissibility indicator, thereby enforcing compliance with operational constraints. MEND introduces an error-bounded inference scheduling at execution that constructs the unmasking schedule by selecting positions with minimal predictive entropy over the constraint-aware action distribution, enhancing collaborative planning optimality under operational constraints. Extensive experimental results in simulation, on real-world maps, and with physical robot teams demonstrate that MEND advances UAV-UGV collaborative planning under operational constraints.

title: T-Rex: Tactile-Reactive Dexterous Manipulation
abstract: The ability to react dynamically to tactile signals has long been considered crucial to agile human-level dexterity. Yet contemporary learning-based VLAs for robotic manipulation generally either overlook the tactile modality or are limited to encoders with static cues, in part due to  the scarcity of diverse training data and standardized evaluation, architectural constraints in current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, and limitations of static tactile encoders. In this paper, we push the frontier of tactile-reactive manipulation addressing all of these limitations. We open-source a large-scale, 100-hour tactile-rich dataset collected via a novel, data-efficient recipe that prioritizes elementary motor primitives. To effectively exploit naturally high-frequency touch signals without sacrificing the existing capabilities of existing VLAs, we introduce a variable-rate Mix-of-Transformer (MoT) architecture equipped with a novel temporal tactile VQ-VAE encoder. We demonstrate the effectiveness of tactile-reactive policies on 12 manipulation tasks requiring delicate force control, deformable object manipulation, achieving over 30% higher average success rate than the strongest baseline.

title: An Adaptive Slow-Fast Framework for Real-Time Anomaly Detection in Autonomous Driving
abstract: Anomaly detection is essential for ensuring the safety and reliability of autonomous driving systems operating in open environments, where rare objects, abnormal behaviors, and long-tail events frequently arise. Conventional perception-based approaches often lack the contextual understanding necessary to interpret complex anomalies, while recent Large Language Model (LLM)-based methods incur substantial computational overhead and exhibit limited integration with geometric sensory modalities. To address these challenges, we propose SOFA, an adaptive slow-fast anomaly detection and reasoning framework that selectively activates multimodal reasoning only when anomalous events are detected. SOFA integrates three key components: 1) a fast LiDAR-based anomaly detection module for efficient real-time perception, 2) a slow VLM-based reasoning module for semantic understanding, and 3) a Time-to-Collision (TTC)-driven switching mechanism that dynamically coordinates the two modules to balance efficiency and reasoning fidelity. To enable systematic evaluation of multimodal anomaly detection and reasoning in real-world driving scenarios, we further construct MAQA, a Multimodal Anomaly Question Answering dataset comprising 16K anomalous objects, synchronized LiDAR-image observations, and reasoning-oriented language annotations. Extensive experiments on MAQA demonstrate that SOFA significantly outperforms baselines in detection accuracy, computational efficiency, and reasoning capability.
